home.hero: A European music network for people who live music in person: artists and bands, curious listeners and people who never miss a gig. We connect scenes across Europe and show you where to play, where to go tonight and who is worth hearing.
home.manifesto_1: "Dead People Activity starts from the ground up: from those who play live music, listen to it and chase it from venue to venue. It is not a magazine or an app: it is the beginning of a European community that wants to grow, one piece at a time and with its own hands. No masters, no algorithms: just people, gigs and scenes keeping each other alive."
home.manifesto_2: This is only the first step, and there is room for anyone who wants to be here: kids at their first show, twenty-year club veterans, artists, listeners, organisers and those who simply never miss a gig. If independent music moves you, this place is yours too. We build the rest together.

a1.page_title: Noise from the streets: why Dead People Activity exists | Dead People Activity
a1.meta: Why European live music needs a map and an archive. The editorial explaining where Dead People Activity begins.
a1.p1: The underground scene exists. The problem is that it disappears. You hear about a gig the next day, when someone posts a photo. A band takes two years to get good and six months to split without leaving a line behind. A venue keeps an entire city alive, then closes and suddenly it is as if it never existed.
a1.p2: We are tired of missing all of this. Dead People Activity starts here: from the desire to keep live music outside the major circuits from fading away. It is not a glossy magazine or another app profiling you to sell advertising. It is a place built from the ground up by people who actually go to gigs.
a1.p3: The most practical need is knowing where to go tonight. That is why the heart of the project is a map: open Europe, choose your city and see what is happening nearby. Gigs, club nights, festivals and DJ sets. Not only the big names found everywhere, but smaller dates that usually travel by word of mouth or inside a closed group.
a1.p4: The map is already online and grows every day, city by city and country by country. It began in Italy and Spain and is expanding across Europe.
a1.p5: Alongside active events, we preserve those that have ended. Bands that split, venues that closed and festivals that vanished are marked [BURIED] and stay here, because a scene is also made of what came before. Documenting it is already a form of resistance.
a1.p6: This is the first step, not the destination. The network grows through people: artists who play, listeners who discover and people who never miss a gig. There is room for everyone, from kids at their first show to those who have spent twenty years in clubs.
a1.p7: If independent music moves you, this place is yours too. Open the map, see what is near you and tell us about any night others should know. We will build the rest together.
a2.page_title: Your first DIY show: a practical guide | Dead People Activity
a2.meta: How to organise a DIY gig or night from scratch: venue, budget, line-up, promotion and door money. A step-by-step guide.
a2.intro: You do not need a thousand-capacity venue or a major-label budget to make something happen. You need a space, a few bands and a willingness to get your hands dirty. Here is how to put on your first night without losing your mind.
a2.p1: Start with what is nearby: a club, social centre, pub with a back room, legal garage or association. Look for places already used to live music so you avoid problems with neighbours and permits. Ask clearly: capacity, sound system, closing time and cost. Sometimes bringing people to the bar is enough.
a2.p2: Do honest sums before saying yes to anyone. Basic costs include venue hire, sound equipment if needed, expenses for the bands—even just fuel and dinner—and printed material. Write everything down. The golden rule: never promise money you are not sure you have. Better to say “pay what you can, we split the takings” than disappear with a loss.
a2.p3: Three bands are ideal for a first show: enough to fill the night, few enough to manage. Mix one act that draws a crowd with two emerging projects, so people discover something new and the room is not empty. Agree on set times and lengths beforehand, not on the night.
a2.p4: One clear poster is worth ten random stories. Date, place, time, bands and price must be understood in two seconds. Print it and put it where the right people go: record shops, other venues and universities. Create the event online, share it in local groups and add the night to the Dead People Activity map—that is what it was made for.
a2.p5: Decide in advance between a fixed price and voluntary contribution. Put someone reliable at the door with change. At the end, count the money in front of everyone and split it as agreed. Transparency is what brings bands and audiences back.
a2.p6: It does not end when the lights go out. Take a few photos and a video, thank the performers and audience, and record what worked and what did not. That night is already part of the memory: tell its story, archive it and the next one will be easier.

a3.page_title: Self-releasing music: tapes, vinyl and CDs without going broke | Dead People Activity
a3.meta: A practical guide to physical self-releases: format, costs, DIY artwork, quantities and distribution for independent artists.
a3.intro: Not many people buy physical music, but those who do genuinely support you and take a piece of your work home. A well-stocked merch table also makes a difference at shows. The real question is not whether to self-release, but what and how much. Let us sort it out.
a3.h1: Cassette: cheap and rooted in the scene
a3.p1: It is the cheapest way to put something physical in people's hands. Each copy costs little, small runs work well and the rough aesthetic belongs in the underground. Downsides: limited audio quality and fewer people own players. Ideal for demos, splits and show-only editions.
a3.p2: CD remains the compromise: good quality, reasonable medium-run costs and easy shipping. The problem is that fewer people listen to them. It makes sense for an older audience or anyone wanting a complete object with booklet and lyrics without spending a fortune.
a3.p3: It is what everyone wants and what costs the most. Pressing times can be long and the unit price only falls with larger runs, so you need confidence that it will sell. Consider it once you have an audience, perhaps using pre-orders to cover costs before pressing.
a3.h4: Artwork: save money and stand out
a3.p4: You do not need an expensive designer. Photocopies, hand screen-printing, stamps and collage: fanzine aesthetics are part of the game and cost little. Take care with the cover, back and credits. Recognisable artwork is worth more than an expensive format printed badly.
a3.p5: Start small with a first release. Selling out and repressing is better than finding unsold boxes in the basement. A numbered limited run is also easier to sell because followers know it is rare.
a3.p6: Three main channels: gigs, where the merch table still sells most; Bandcamp for online orders; and independent record shops on consignment. Set a fair price that covers costs and leaves a margin without overdoing it. This is not about getting rich—it is about keeping a scene alive.
